body.text: Mahjong night has a reputation for needing an expert, but the only thing you must sort out before the first night is which version of the game you're playing. Everything else is hosting: a table, a pot of tea, good light and a standing date.

This guide doesn't teach any version's rules. It helps you choose one, equip it, run a first evening that's meant to be practice and turn it into a tradition. It starts with the one decision that saves you money.
Mahjong means several games
Mahjong is a family of related tile games, and the sets, reference materials and rules differ depending on where and how you learn. You're most likely to meet three:

items: **American mahjong.** Usually played with a card of approved hands that is published periodically, and a set that includes jokers.
**Chinese mahjong, including regional styles such as Hong Kong.** Several styles, each with its own scoring and conventions. Sets typically don't include the jokers found in American sets.
**Japanese Riichi mahjong.** Its own rules and scoring, with set features of its own.

body.text: A set bought for one style may be missing pieces another style needs, and a friend who learned one way will play differently from someone who learned another. Agree on the version with your group before anything goes in a cart.
Find your teacher

Somebody at the table needs to know the game. Look for a friend or relative who plays, or for local clubs, community classes and online tutorials. Most teach one specific version, so confirm which before you sign up and stick with it while you learn, because switching styles midway is confusing.
If nobody in your group plays, take a lesson first and host after a couple of practice rounds. A table of beginners laughing at their own mistakes is a perfectly good first night.
What to have on the table

essentials: A complete set made for the version you're playing
A table with room for four and chairs you can sit in for a few hours
Good light, because tile symbols are small
The current reference card, book or rules sheet for your version
Someone who can teach the basics, or a plan to learn together first
optional: A playing mat or soft cover to cushion the tiles and quiet the clatter
Racks, and pushers where your version and set use them
A carrying case for storage and travel
Side trays or small tables for tea and snacks

body.text: You probably already own a sturdy table, chairs, mugs, small bowls, napkins and a lamp, and a tablecloth or felt-ish blanket can stand in for a mat. Borrowing a set for the first night or two is a good plan if a friend or relative has one. A better set, a fancier case and themed accessories can wait until you've played a few times.
If you do buy a set

items: **A beginner set suited to your version.** This is the big purchase, and prices vary widely with materials and extras. Check that the listing names your version, see what's included and prefer tiles that are easy to read. Larger tiles are kind to tired eyes.

**Racks and pushers.** Racks are commonly sold with American-style sets; other styles may play without them, and pushers only matter if your version and set call for them. Check what your set already includes.
**A playing mat.** It softens the sound, protects the tiles and your table, and gives the game a defined little stage.
**The current reference card or book.** These are version-specific and, for some styles, updated periodically. Buy the current one for your agreed version, not whichever looks prettiest.

body.text: Before you click buy: does the listing name your version? For American mahjong, does the set include at least eight jokers? Does the reference card or book match that version? If any answer is 'not sure', ask the seller or your teacher first.
Your first night, step by step
Keep it short, warm and clearly labeled as practice. Two good hours beat four tired ones.

items: A week before: confirm the version, the date and the guest list, and ask about allergies and dietary needs.
Two days before: check that your set is complete and the reference card or book is the right one, and do a dry run of your setup.
On the day: mat down, lamp on, tea and snacks on side trays rather than the playing surface. Skip greasy snacks near the tiles.
At arrival: drinks and snacks first. Say plainly that tonight is practice and questions are welcome.
First hour: your teacher walks through the pieces and the flow of a turn, and you play slowly with hands open so everyone can ask.
After a break: play a more normal round if people are ready, or stop while it's still fun.
Before anyone leaves: pick the next date. A standing slot is what turns one night into a tradition.

body.text: If something goes sideways

items: **People are playing by different rules.** Pause, agree on one set for the night and write it down. Mixing rules from different styles in one game is the usual cause.
**A tile seems to be missing.** Check the set before guests arrive. If something has gone astray, ask your teacher how your version handles it rather than improvising.
**Someone feels overwhelmed.** Slow down, keep hands open and let them watch a round.
**You don't have four players.** Keep a backup like a card game or a craft, and let the extra guest observe and learn.
**It's loud.** Add a mat or a thicker cloth. The clatter is part of the charm, but your neighbors may disagree.

body.text: Turning it into a tradition

A game gives everyone something to do with their hands and a reason to stay put. Conversation arrives in waves between turns, so the quiet friend gets room and the chatty one gets a break. It's also kinder to people who don't drink and easier on your ears than a restaurant.

Pick a rhythm you'll honestly keep, such as every other Friday or the first Sunday of the month. Rotate hosts so nobody carries the whole load, and keep a tiny ritual like the same tea or the same opening toast. Over time it becomes less 'what are we doing?' and more 'see you Friday.'
Playing with respect
Mahjong is part of family life and community tradition for many people, so it deserves more than a themed-party treatment.

items: **Skip costumes, props and stereotypes.** Let the game, the company and the snacks speak for themselves.
**Learn from people who grew up with it, if you can.** Ask what the game means to them, and listen.
**Name the version you're playing.** 'We're learning American mahjong' or 'we're playing Riichi' shows you know there are differences.
**Follow the house rules of whoever is teaching you,** especially in their home, and treat the tiles gently. They're often valued and sometimes handed down.
**Stay curious.** Mahjong is played in many countries with a lot of local variation, and its history is worth reading about in reliable sources.

body.text: Message your group chat: 'Does anyone play mahjong, and which version?' You may find a hidden expert, a borrowable set, or a table of friends who've all been wanting to learn.

body.title: Before you buy a set
body.dek: Pick one set, not all of them: check which version it is made for and what it includes, and match the card to your version. The listing is the source for price and stock.
